reason: Attacked on wording, edition and locator, and it survives all three. The decisive check was a Google Books snippet of the named edition itself (The Lais of Marie de France, Glyn Sheridan Burgess, 1986, page 41), which prints ‘has a duty not to remain silent : rather should one be happy to reveal such talents. When a truly beneficial thing is heard by many people’, so both the disputed clause order and the following sentence are the Penguin text. Archive.org metadata for laisofmariedefra0000burg confirms that item is the Penguin 1986 edition, ISBN 0140444769, so the evidence url points at the edition named. A transcription of the Penguin text shows the sentence standing immediately under the heading PROLOGUE, which confirms ‘opening sentence’. Four further scholarly quotations (Bloch, The Anonymous Marie de France, p. 36; Whalen, A Companion to Marie de France, p. 4; Gilbert, Norton Critical Edition, 2015; Caws, 1995) give the identical wording. I did find a rival reading, ‘rather one should be happy to reveal such talents’, in The Medieval Translator 4 (1994, p. 56), in Yale French Studies 86 to 87 (p. 172) and in one ResearchGate paper citing ‘1988: 41’, and I chased it because a single-word inversion is exactly this track’s failure mode. It does not stand: the snippet of the 1986 book itself reads ‘rather should one be happy’, and the three dissenters are secondary quotations, two of them of the same lineage. Not shipped, not banned, Marie de France stands at zero of three, and no other May proposal uses her. In scope: c. 1170, verse lai, not scripture despite naming God. Source line leads with the name, 119 characters, no dash, translation in parentheses. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. betterCitation only adds the page the snippet confirms, taking the line to 126 characters, still inside 140. One thing the board should settle rather than me: Burgess and Busby render the Lais in prose, so a verse work ships here as an unbroken sentence. Rule seven is edition-relative (‘in the lineation of the edition named’) so this complies as written, but the card would read more honestly with a note saying the named translation is prose and no lineation is owed, which by the precedent of carry-in 03-fict-08 means ruling it CORRECTED rather than VERIFIED. That is a note, not a defect in the citation.
